name: Egypt
summary: The kingdom of the Nile, unified around 3100 BCE and ruled by pharaohs for nearly three thousand years. The pyramids of Giza and the Step Pyramid at Saqqara belong to its Old Kingdom; hieroglyphic writing on papyrus, a 365-day civil calendar, monumental temples and the belief in a judged afterlife run through the whole span.

fell.text: Cambyses II of Persia defeated the last king of the Twenty-sixth Dynasty at Pelusium in 525 BCE and Egypt became a Persian province, with native rule returning only in brief intervals until Alexander.

name: Indus Valley Civilization
summary: The Harappan cities: Mohenjo-daro, Harappa, Dholavira and hundreds of smaller towns on the Indus and its lost neighbour, the Ghaggar-Hakra. Planned street grids, covered drains, standardized brick and weights, and a script that is still unread.

fell.text: The cities emptied over two centuries as rivers shifted and the monsoon weakened; there was no conqueror, and village life continued.

name: Semitic-speaking peoples
summary: The peoples of Arabia and the Syrian steppe who spoke the Semitic languages, ancestors of the Akkadians, Amorites, Canaanites, Arameans and Arabs. Before the first states here, the map shows the region their languages covered: herders, caravan traders and oasis farmers rather than a kingdom.

name: Sumer
summary: The city-states of southern Mesopotamia: Uruk, Ur, Lagash, Kish and their rivals. Cuneiform writing on clay appears here around 3200 BCE, alongside irrigated barley fields, temple economies, the potter's wheel and the earliest known literature.

fell.text: Sargon of Akkad conquered the Sumerian cities and folded them into the first empire. Sumerian survived as a language of learning for another two thousand years.

name: Assyria
summary: From a city-state on the Tigris, Assyria grew by stages into the largest empire the world had seen, ruling from Nineveh and Nimrud over lands from the Nile to the Persian Gulf. Standing armies, provincial governors, a royal road network, and the library of Ashurbanipal, which preserved the Epic of Gilgamesh.

fell.text: A coalition of Babylonians and Medes sacked Nineveh in 612 BCE; the last Assyrian king fell at Harran three years later.

name: Kingdom of Kush
summary: The Nubian kingdom on the Nile south of Egypt, ruled first from Napata and then from Meroë. Its kings ruled Egypt itself as the Twenty-fifth Dynasty, and Meroë became a center of iron working with its own alphabetic script.

fell.text: Meroë declined as trade routes shifted to the Red Sea; an Aksumite campaign around 350 marks its conventional end.

name: North American Pacific foraging, hunting and fishing peoples
Patagonian shellfish and marine mammal hunters
Achaemenid Empire
summary: The Persian empire of Cyrus, Darius and Xerxes, stretching from the Aegean and Egypt to the Indus. Satrapies with local autonomy, the Royal Road with its relay couriers, a gold and silver coinage, Aramaic as the language of administration, and the palace city of Persepolis.

fell.text: Alexander of Macedon defeated Darius III at Gaugamela in 331 BCE and burned Persepolis the next year.

name: Empire of Alexander
summary: Alexander's conquest of the Persian empire in eleven years, from Greece to the Indus and Egypt. It did not outlive him, but the cities he founded and the Greek language he spread shaped the Hellenistic world for three centuries.

fell.text: Alexander died in Babylon in June 323 BCE without a clear heir; his generals divided the empire in forty years of war.

name: Maya
summary: Not one state but a mosaic of city-states in the Yucatán and the highlands to its south: Tikal, Calakmul, Palenque, Copán, later Chichén Itzá and Mayapán. A fully developed writing system, the Long Count calendar, an accurate Venus table and the concept of zero, recorded in carved stone and painted books. The southern cities emptied in the ninth century; the northern ones carried on until the Spanish conquest.
capital: Tikal, Calakmul, Palenque, Chichén Itzá and others

fell.text: The Spanish took the last independent Maya kingdom, the Itza capital at Nojpetén, in 1697, a century and a half after the conquest of Yucatán began.

name: Maurya Empire
summary: The first empire to hold most of the Indian subcontinent, founded by Chandragupta and ruled at its height by Ashoka, whose edicts carved on rocks and pillars are the earliest deciphered Indian writing. Ashoka's patronage carried Buddhism across Asia.

fell.text: The last Maurya emperor was killed by his general Pushyamitra Shunga, who founded a new dynasty in Magadha.

name: Han Dynasty
summary: Four centuries that fixed the shape of Chinese civilization: a Confucian civil service, the Silk Road opened to the west, paper, the seismoscope, and the Records of the Grand Historian. The Han name is still the word for China's largest ethnic group.

fell.text: Cao Pi accepted the abdication of the last Han emperor in 220; China split into the Three Kingdoms.

name: Roman Empire
summary: The Mediterranean world under one rule, from Augustus to the permanent division of 395. Concrete, aqueducts, roads that are still in use, a body of law that underlies most of Europe's legal systems, and Latin, the parent of the Romance languages.

fell.text: On the death of Theodosius I the empire was divided between his sons and never reunited.

name: Kingdom of Aksum
summary: A trading kingdom in the Ethiopian highlands, minting its own gold coins and raising monolithic stelae over thirty meters tall. Aksum adopted Christianity around 330 under King Ezana, one of the first states to do so, and wrote in the Ge'ez script still used in Ethiopian liturgy.

fell.text: Red Sea trade passed to Arab merchants and the capital was abandoned; the Zagwe dynasty took over the highlands.
The Vietnamese took Vijaya in 1471; the last Cham principality, Panduranga, was absorbed by the Nguyen emperor Minh Mang in 1832.
The Northern Wei conquered the Northern Liang in 439, the last of the sixteen, and united the north.

name: Gupta Empire
summary: Northern India's classical age. Under the Guptas, Aryabhata computed pi and the length of the year, the decimal place-value system with a zero came into use, Kalidasa wrote his plays, and the Ajanta caves were painted.

fell.text: Hun invasions from the northwest and the breakaway of provincial governors dissolved the empire into regional kingdoms.

name: Byzantine Empire
summary: The Roman empire as it continued in the Greek East for a thousand years, ruled from Constantinople. Justinian's law code, the dome of Hagia Sophia, Greek fire, the preservation of classical Greek literature, and the Cyrillic alphabet, which grew from the mission to the Slavs.

fell.text: Mehmed II took Constantinople on 29 May 1453 after a fifty-three day siege.

name: Western Roman Empire
summary: The Latin half of the divided empire, ruled from Milan and then Ravenna. It lost Britain, most of Gaul, Spain and Africa to Germanic kingdoms in eighty years, and ended when Odoacer deposed Romulus Augustulus in 476.

fell.text: Odoacer deposed the boy emperor Romulus Augustulus and sent the imperial regalia to Constantinople.
Xiao Yan deposed the last Qi emperor in 502 and founded the Liang.
Chen Baxian took the throne in 557 after the Hou Jing rebellion had wrecked the dynasty.
Sui armies took Jiankang in 589 and reunited China.

name: Abbasid Caliphate
summary: The caliphate that moved the Islamic world's capital to Baghdad and presided over its golden age. The House of Wisdom translated Greek, Persian and Indian science; al-Khwarizmi wrote the book that gave algebra its name; paper mills, hospitals and observatories spread across the empire.

fell.text: Hulagu's Mongol army sacked Baghdad in February 1258 and killed the caliph al-Musta'sim.
The Karakhanids took Bukhara in 999 while the Ghaznavids, once Samanid slave-governors, took Khurasan south of the Oxus.
The last Seljuk sultan of Iraq, Tughril III, was killed in 1194 by the Khwarazmshah Tekish, who took Iran.

name: Mongol Empire
summary: The largest contiguous land empire in history, built in two generations from the steppe. Under the Pax Mongolica, trade and ideas moved from China to the Black Sea along secured roads with relay stations; the Yam postal system, paper money and gunpowder travelled with them.

fell.text: The empire had split into four khanates in the civil wars after 1259; the death of Kublai Khan in 1294 removed the last ruler the others acknowledged.

name: Mali Empire
summary: The West African empire of Sundiata and Mansa Musa, rich on Bambuk gold and the trans-Saharan trade. Timbuktu and Djenné became centers of Islamic learning whose manuscript libraries survive today.

fell.text: Eclipsed by Songhai, which took Timbuktu in 1468, Mali shrank to its Mandinka heartland and was finally broken up by the Bamana of Segu around 1670.
Ayutthaya made Sukhothai a vassal in 1378 and a province when its royal line ended in 1438.

name: Ottoman Empire
summary: Six centuries of rule from Anatolia over the Balkans, the Middle East and North Africa. Constantinople taken in 1453, the mosques of Sinan, the Topkapı workshops, coffeehouses, a legal code that blended sharia with sultanic law, and the millet system for its many faiths.
region: Anatolia, Balkans, Middle East, North Africa

fell.text: The sultanate was abolished by the Grand National Assembly on 1 November 1922; the Republic of Turkey was proclaimed the next year.
Oda Nobunaga drove the last Ashikaga shogun out of Kyoto in 1573; the map goes on as Japan of the Warring States.

name: Ming Dynasty
summary: The dynasty that rebuilt the Great Wall in the form seen today, built the Forbidden City, and sent Zheng He's treasure fleets as far as East Africa. Blue-and-white porcelain, the Yongle Encyclopedia, and a population that doubled.

fell.text: Peasant rebels took Beijing in April 1644 and the last Ming emperor hanged himself; the Manchu Qing entered the city weeks later.
Afonso de Albuquerque took the city in August 1511; the sultan fled and his heirs founded Johor.

name: Aztec Empire
summary: The Triple Alliance of Tenochtitlan, Texcoco and Tlacopan, ruling central Mexico from an island city of perhaps 200,000 people, larger than any city in Spain at the time. Chinampa raised fields, causeways and aqueducts, and a solar calendar of 365 days.

fell.text: Tenochtitlan fell to Hernán Cortés and his Tlaxcalan allies on 13 August 1521 after a siege and a smallpox epidemic.

name: Inca Empire
summary: Tawantinsuyu, the largest state in the pre-Columbian Americas, ruled from Cusco. A road network of some 40,000 km with suspension bridges, terraced farming and freeze-dried storage, record keeping on knotted quipu cords, and stonework fitted without mortar.

fell.text: Francisco Pizarro captured the emperor Atahualpa at Cajamarca in 1532 and executed him the next year; resistance continued at Vilcabamba until 1572.

name: Songhai Empire
summary: Songhai grew from the river city of Gao to take over the Niger bend from Mali under Sunni Ali and Askia Muhammad. Timbuktu's Sankoré scholars flourished under its rule; a Moroccan army with firearms ended it at Tondibi in 1591.

fell.text: A Moroccan expeditionary force armed with muskets defeated the Songhai army at Tondibi in March 1591.

name: Emirate of the White Sheep Turks
Mississaugas of the Credit First Nation
Nahua ( Morelos, Puebla, Tlaxcala, Veracruz, Hidalgo, San Luis Potosi)
Seminole Tribe of Florida (Big Cypress Reservation)
Mughal Empire
summary: Babur's dynasty ruled most of the Indian subcontinent for two centuries. Akbar's religious tolerance and land-revenue reforms, the Taj Mahal and Red Fort, miniature painting, and Persian as the court language that fed into Urdu.

fell.text: The last emperor, Bahadur Shah Zafar, was exiled by the British after the uprising of 1857; the Crown took direct rule of India the next year.
The Peshwa surrendered to the East India Company in 1818 after the Third Anglo-Maratha War.

aliases: Independent State of Papua New Guinea
